title: Merged Departure Board
story: A small station's departure screen merges two feeds, trains and buses, into one list sorted by time. Times are minutes after midnight, so 6:05 is 365.
Departures that share a time show as rows like 365, 365, but the screen has room for one row per time. Its tiny controller cannot afford a second list, so it must clean up the one it has.
task: Write dedupeBoard(times). times is sorted from earliest to latest. Change it in place so it holds each distinct time exactly once, still sorted, and nothing else. Return nothing.
Do not build a second list. Overwrite values inside times, then cut off the leftover tail (in JavaScript set times.length; in Python use del times[k:], where k is how many times you kept).
constraints: times is sorted in non-decreasing order.

examples.explanation: 365 appears twice and 455 three times. Keep one of each: 365, 410, 455, 520. The list shrinks from 7 entries to 4.
No time repeats, so the list is unchanged.

hints: Look at [365, 365, 410]. Since the list is sorted, where can a repeat of 365 be? Could one appear after 410?
In a sorted list, equal values sit together. A value is new exactly when it differs from the last value you kept.
Picture two fingers. One reads every entry left to right. The other marks the next free spot in the cleaned front part. The writing finger never gets ahead of the reading one.
Keep a write index w, starting at 0. For each read index r: if w is 0 or times[r] differs from times[w - 1], copy it to times[w] and add 1 to w. At the end, shorten the list to length w.
bruteForce: Walk the list and delete each entry equal to the one before it (splice in JavaScript, del or pop(i) in Python).

Every delete shifts all later entries left. 10,000 entries that are almost all repeats means close to 10,000 deletes, about 50 million moves. Writing each kept entry once, straight to its final spot, avoids the shifting.

js: * @param {number[]} times  sorted; change it in place

tests.note: growing runs; the tail must be cut off

js: let w = 0; // next free slot in the cleaned front part
times.length = w; // cut off the leftover tail
py: w = 0  # next free slot in the cleaned front part
del times[w:]  # cut off the leftover tail
walkthrough: Split the list into a cleaned front, times[0..w-1], holding each time once, and the unread rest. A read index r scans everything. Since the list is sorted, an entry is new exactly when it differs from the last kept one, times[w - 1].
• r = 1, 365. Same as the last kept. Skip.
Writing never overtakes reading (w ≤ r), so you never overwrite an entry you still need.
solution.timeWhy: One pass, and each entry is read once and written at most once.
solution.spaceWhy: Two indexes. The list is reused in place.
solution.takeaway: To filter a list in place, use a read pointer that visits everything and a write pointer marking the end of the kept part. Keep an item by copying it to the write pointer, then trim the tail.
